On the actual code: this is a standard OpenAI Python SDK call pointed at a third-party proxy (`api.llmapi.ai`) rather than OpenAI's own endpoint, using `base_url` to redirect requests. This pattern — swapping `base_url` and `api_key` while keeping the OpenAI client — is the common way to hit OpenAI-compatible endpoints from providers like Ollama, vLLM, LiteLLM proxies, and Google's Gemini compatibility layer.[1][2][3]

## What the Code Does

The script instantiates an `OpenAI` client but overrides `base_url` to ``, meaning every request goes to that third-party service instead of `api.openai.com`. The `api_key` field is just a placeholder string `"YOUR_API_KEY"` — you'd need to replace this with a real key issued by that specific provider, since OpenAI's own keys won't authenticate against a different host. The `model` parameter, `"gemini-3-pro-image"`, is passed straight through to whatever backend `api.llmapi.ai` maps that string to — the OpenAI SDK itself doesn't validate model names, it just forwards them in the request body.[2][3]

## Gemini Compatibility Caveats

If the intent is to reach Google's actual Gemini models through the OpenAI SDK, Google offers its own compatibility endpoint at ``, which supports the Chat Completions and Embeddings APIs specifically. However, Gemini's OpenAI compatibility layer is limited — it doesn't support the newer Responses API, and most non-OpenAI providers only implement Chat Completions compatibility, not the full feature set. Since your code targets a third-party aggregator (`llmapi.ai`) rather than Google directly, the actual behavior of a model name like `gemini-3-pro-image` — including whether it returns text, image URLs, or errors — depends entirely on that aggregator's own routing and documentation, which isn't something I can verify without knowing their specific API contract.[4][1]
